title: One dish you've cooked before
allegory: A capstone is like cooking for a dinner party three Saturdays away: the cooks who shine make one dish they have cooked before, improve one thing about it, and plate it with an honest note, rather than attempting a whole new cuisine.

chapters.name: The banquet plan
chapters.note: W12: new method, three questions, one talk

cap.1: Week 12. You plan something dazzling: a brand-new method, three big questions, a talk. Three Saturdays later you have a half-working notebook.
cap.2: The capstone runs W12 to W14: three Saturdays, not one. W12 is already project time, and /checkpoint starts asking about it at W8.
cap.3: The usual failure is scope, not skill: new tooling eats the time meant for results, and there is nothing to show when the talk arrives.

props.label: note: what's in it, and what isn't

cap.1: A cook has three Saturdays before a dinner party. The ones who shine make one dish they've cooked before, improve one thing, and plate it with a note.
cap.2: One question, small enough for three Saturdays, answered with a technique you've already implemented: patching, an SAE latent study, or a small eval.
cap.3: Reusing working code moves the risk from 'does my pipeline run' to 'what does the result mean', which is the part worth presenting.

cap.1: Start from your shelf, not the shop: something you've already built. Point it at one new question, spend three Saturdays, then give the talk.
cap.2: Patching (W8), an SAE latent study (W8), a small eval (W11), or a replication: reproduce one figure from one paper, then say one honest thing about it.
cap.3: ARENA's chapter 4 sections are each built around one or two recent papers with the replication half scaffolded: the shortest path from a paper to a presentable result.

chapters.name: Where Saturdays go
chapters.title: Three Saturdays, two plans: starting fresh, then reusing a technique (illustrative)

cap.1: Same three Saturdays, two plans. Starting fresh spends most of them getting tools to run. Reusing a technique spends them on the answer.
cap.2: An illustrative split: a new method can eat two Saturdays before the first real result, while reused code gets you to experiments almost at once and leaves slack.
cap.3: The lesson from TARA's calendar: projects that finish reuse a technique from a Saturday you actually did, rather than starting something new in W12.

chapters.name: Question, not topic

right.title: A question
lines: 'does this latent fire on those prompts?'
a yes, a no, or a surprise

chapters.verdict: A question has an answer you can reach; a topic only has more topic.

cap.1: Scope it as a question, not a topic. 'SAEs and deception' has no finish line; 'does this latent fire on those prompts' can be answered by week 14.
cap.2: A good capstone question has a concrete result shape: a patching heatmap, a latent's top activating examples, a score on a small eval set, one reproduced figure.
cap.3: Decide in advance what each outcome would mean. A clean negative from a well-scoped question is still a finding you can present.

cap.1: On 12 December you give the talk. Show what you found, and say one honest thing about what it does and doesn't show.
cap.2: The final presentation, with 11 of 14 Saturdays attended, is the pass condition. A small finished result beats a large unfinished one.
cap.3: State claims at the strength the evidence supports: which model, which prompts, which layers, and what the method localises versus what it leaves open.

cap.1: Finishing one small, true result is how you learn to do research on AI, and understanding or steering a model starts with findings like that.
cap.2: The capstone turns weeks of exercises into one piece of evidence you produced yourself, start to finish: a question, a method and a caveat.
cap.3: Interpretability and alignment progress is built from small, well-scoped, checkable claims. Practising that shape now is the skill that transfers.

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: 3 - newtech*learn - parts*0.75 - 0.5 >= 0.75 ? 'finishable, with room for surprises' : (3 - newtech*learn - parts*0.75 - 0.5 >= 0 ? 'tight: one surprise and it slips' : 'over budget: cut a question or reuse a technique')

caption.1: Set how many techniques you'd learn from scratch and how many questions you're asking. Watch the slack bar: below zero, the talk arrives before the answer.
caption.2: Toy costs (illustrative): you set how long a new technique takes; each question costs three quarters of a Saturday and the talk half of one. Reuse zeroes the first bar.
caption.3: New tooling is the hardest cost to estimate, so keep slack positive even with the learning guess doubled. Reusing a technique removes that term entirely.

hamming.what: The capstone is one question, small enough to answer in three Saturdays, using a technique you have already implemented, presented in a final talk.
hamming.when: Weeks 12 to 14, with /checkpoint asking about it from week 8 and the talk on 12 December 2026.
hamming.why: Reusing a technique you built moves the risk from getting tools to run onto what the result means, which is what lets projects finish.

object.title: The three-Saturday rail
object.subtitle: Three Saturdays and a talk, threaded on one question that runs through every block.

items.label: Saturday 1: a technique off your shelf, running
Saturday 2: the experiment that answers it

cap.1: Three Saturdays and a talk. The tube running through every block is your one question: the same one all the way.
cap.2: One suggested split of W12 to W14. The point is the thread: one question from the first block to the last.
cap.3: A single, fixed question keeps every Saturday's work cumulative instead of starting over.

cap.1: Saturday one: take a technique off your shelf and get it running on the new question. No new tooling.
cap.2: Patching, an SAE latent study or a small eval you already implemented, pointed at new prompts or a new model.
cap.3: Reuse turns setup into a check that known results still reproduce before you ask the new question.

cap.1: Saturday two, the tallest block: the experiment that answers the question. This is where the time should go.
cap.2: Run it, look at the outputs, and note what surprised you while there is still time to follow it.
cap.3: Decide beforehand what each outcome would mean, so a negative result is still interpretable.

cap.1: Saturday three: caveats, then slides. Then 12 December and the talk, the tallest block of all.
cap.2: With 11 of 14 Saturdays attended, the talk is the pass condition. A finished small result is what you bring.
cap.3: Say one honest thing about what the result does and doesn't show; that is part of the result.
